transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Dev Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Archon CTO), Tom Reynolds (Archon Platform), Lena Chu (Archon ML)

Summary (auto): quick demo focused on edge cases: long context (>64k), high TPS (target ~300 TPS), streaming behavior under client backpressure and timeouts. Showed Console, API patterns, and Redwood Optimize recommendations. Agreed next steps: pricing, streaming best-practices, run benchmarks.

Topics: long context handling; KV/prefix cache; batching and throughput math; streaming backpressure; request & token timeouts; Dedicated sizing; security considerations (VPC/KMS, audit logs)

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, i'm sofia from Redwood, with Dev on the SE side.
[00:06] Priya: Hi, Priya here, CTO at Archon Health. we've been looking at long-context summarization for medical records and need to understand tail behaviour.
[00:12] Tom: Tom, platform eng, curious about implications at 200-400 TPS steady state.
[00:16] Dev: great, yeah we'll focus demo on three edge cases: long context (64k+), high TPS load, and streaming backpressure/timeouts.
[00:25] Lena: quick Q: are you demoing hosted or dedicated?
[00:28] Sofia: both; we'll show Console for hosted metrics and then discuss Dedicated sizing since you mentioned 300 TPS.
[00:34] [00:34] Dev: starting with long context. so our runtime supports models with 64k windows (depending on model). we do KV prefix caching to avoid re-encoding large unchanged prefixes. in practice you can keep the patient history in the KV cache and only send deltas.
[00:46] Priya: when you say KV cache, is that per-session? how many sessions before memory pressure?
[00:52] Dev: good q: KV cache is per-request context saved for reuse; on Dedicated we allocate per-GPU cache pools and evict based on LRU and usage heuristics. you can cap total cached tokens per-deployment. we've seen stable behaviour up to thousands of sessions with a tuned eviction policy.
[01:08] Tom: and what's the memory hit for 64k tokens? like per-request memory?
[01:12] Dev: depends on quantization and model. with 8-bit quant and kernel-level optimizations, a 64k context can be kept but you pay more KV memory; for H100/A100 class nodes we typically provision larger GPU memory or shard across nodes. we also support prefix compaction: we compress older parts of the context to reduce footprint.
[01:28] Priya: ok ok, that makes sense. how about latency when the model has to rehydrate the KV cache?
[01:33] Dev: rehydration introduces a small p95 bump; we do prefetching for hot sessions. for most clients p95 stays within your SLO if you have Dedicated. in hosted, there's a small cold penalty.
[01:43] [01:43] Sofia: moving to high TPS: you said 300 TPS target, we ran the numbers earlier: if average response length is 150 tokens, at 300 TPS that's 45k tokens/sec. batching and token throughput then drive GPU sizing.
[01:56] Tom: what batching strategy would you recommend? synchronous or continuous batching?
[01:59] Dev: our runtime uses continuous batching; it aggregates open requests up to latency SLO and throughput targets. you can set max batch size, max latency window in the route config. for high TPS we tune to larger batches and aggressive token-level batching so throughput improves.
[02:14] Lena: any guidance on concurrency limits per connection?
[02:17] Dev: concurrency is a layer above: we provide worker pools; Recommended approach is to keep per-connection concurrency moderate and scale horizontally. we also support request shaping via Smart Routing to route to cheaper model variants when under heavy load.
[02:27] Priya: can you show the Console metrics for a sample high-tps run?
[02:30] Sofia: yep switching to the Console: bear with me, screen share.
[02:35] [02:35] Sofia: here's a demo run we did: steady-state 320 TPS, 95 token avg, p99 latency ~420ms on Dedicated pool (8x A100 equivalent). you can see batching spikes and token-per-second charts.
[02:48] Tom: how do you handle backpressure when clients can't keep up with streaming chunks? we've got mobile clients with flaky networks.
[02:53] Dev: two patterns: server-side buffering and backpressure-aware streams. with WebSocket streaming we chunk at configurable sizes (e.g., 256 tokens per chunk) and respect TCP backpressure; we also expose a streaming control API so client can request pause/resume. if the client is extremely slow we fallback to full-response (non-streaming) with retries or drop to smaller chunking.
[03:12] Lena: and what about timeouts: we have requirements to fail fast if response exceeds 10s for interactive UIs.
[03:18] Dev: route-level timeouts enforce request timeout and per-token deadlines. you can set short client-facing timeouts (10s) and have the server continue a background compute and return a later webhook, but that complicates UX. we also support chunk-level timeouts plus configurable retry policies.
[03:32] Priya: is there a risk of double-charging if retries happen?
[03:35] Sofia: we surface idempotency tokens in the API. if you replay with same idempotency key we dedupe on the service side and avoid double billing.
[03:42] [03:42] Tom: show us a failing scenario: streaming backpressure + high TPS causing timeouts?
[03:46] Dev: sure: here's a synthetic test we ran: heavy sustained TPS (400) with 20% of clients artificially slowed to 200ms chunk RTT. the runtime pushed back by increasing batching latency for those clients and routed new requests to other pools. we also tripped a backpressure threshold and switched streaming to buffered responses for slow clients. latency SLOs for the rest of the fleet were preserved.
[04:09] Priya: what are the knobs to tune: batch size, max-latency-ms, chunk-size, prefetch-window?
[04:14] Dev: exactly those, plus cache eviction thresholds and fallback routing policies. Redwood Optimize can analyze traffic and suggest tuning values by workload.
[04:22] Lena: quick question about streaming protocols: do you support SSE and WebSocket? what about HTTP/2 chunked?
[04:28] Sofia: we support HTTP streaming, SSE, WebSocket; SDKs handle reconnection. HTTP/2 chunked is supported via our streaming endpoints but websocket is preferred for bi-directional control.
[04:36] [04:36] Priya: security: since this is PHI, we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. how mature are those features?
[04:42] Dev: on Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS keys and HSM integrations; audit logs are available in Console with immutable retention options. we also support VPC peering and private control plane for regulated workloads.
[04:54] Tom: any SOC/ISO compliance artifacts we can review?
[04:57] Sofia: yes we'll send our security pack (SOC2, ISO cert docs, penetration test summary).
[05:02] [05:02] Dev: returning to performance, one more important thing: timeouts vs streaming: if you set a client-facing 10s timeout but server is mid-stream the client can cancel; we recommend small chunk sizes and soft timeouts plus server-side continuation for webhook fallback for async UX.
[05:18] Priya: can you walk through a code example for streaming with backpressure awareness?
[05:21] Dev: sure: (Dev talks through a pseudo-code WebSocket client: open socket, send request with idempotency key, handle onmessage append chunks, if network lag > 500ms request smaller chunk_size, send pause/resume control messages).
[05:40] [05:40] Tom: any pre-built client libs?
[05:42] Sofia: we have JS/Go/Python SDKs with built-in backpressure utilities and a sample mobile reconnection pattern. we'll share those links.
[05:50] Lena: for the benchmark run, how do we simulate realistic long-context loads?
[05:53] Dev: we recommend mixed request sizes: 10% long-context sessions (40-64k tokens), 70% medium (1-5k), 20% short. use our load harness which supports KV cache warmup so you measure realistic cache hit rates.
[06:08] Priya: what about cost math: if we run 300 TPS steady state, any estimate?
[06:12] Sofia: rough rule: tokens/sec * model cost factor / batching efficiency. we'll produce a Dedicated capacity estimate in the follow-up; for example our earlier run with 320 TPS and 95 token avg needed a 8-GPU pool and had estimated monthly committed cost X (we'll put numbers in the pricing doc).
[06:28] [06:28] Tom: how do model rollouts work under heavy load? can you canary a new model variant?
[06:32] Dev: yes: Console supports canary rollouts by percentage and routing by policy (latency, cost). if the canary degrades, automatic fallback to previous variant occurs. we also support A/B and shadow traffic.
[06:42] Priya: ok: last piece on reliability: what do we do for long-running background completions if clients disconnect?
[06:47] Dev: you can use our async jobs API: request returns job id, we continue compute server-side and post results via webhook or let clients poll. logs include token-level progress.
[06:57] [06:57] Sofia: wrapping up demo, show the Optimize tab: it flagged that for this workload you should enable aggressive batching, prefix caching, and quantize to 8-bit for cost savings with minimal quality loss.
[07:12] Sofia: i'm going to recap action items and next steps.
[07:14] Priya: sounds good.
[07:16] Sofia: next steps: send pricing and security pack, share streaming best-practices, schedule benchmark run.
[07:21] Tom: we'll confirm dataset and window for the benchmark.
[07:23] Lena: thanks, this was helpful.
[07:25] Sofia: thanks all: we'll follow up via email.

Notes about transcription quality: some terms were transcribed incorrectly (Redwood Optimize as 'Redwood Opitmize' in places, 'KV cache' sometimes 'K-V cache'); names occasionally merged. Document intentionally preserves spoken disfluencies.

End of meeting.
